clue.text: It's a bloomer, employing 41 in operation

indicators.note: the number is placed in the middle of the abbreviation for operation

parts.note: XLI is 41 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A gardener's flower somehow involves forty-one people in a surgical operation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomer' suggests a blunder, but here it is literally a thing that blooms; 'employing ... in' signals the container. Roman numerals are a common crossword source of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowslip-like primrose is a flowering plant, and any flower is jokingly a bloomer.

clue.text: Compel initial 20% reduction in negotiable reforms

indicators.note: reforms says the remaining letters are rearranged into a new shape
initial says the letters cut away come from the very start of the word
reduction in says letters are cut away from the word that follows

parts.note: a fifth of a ten-letter word is two letters

explanation.surface: A government forces through a first fifth cut as part of flexible reforms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Initial' and 'reduction in' together cut the opening fifth (two letters, NE) from NEGOTIABLE, leaving GOTIABLE for 'reforms' to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To obligate someone is to bind or force them to act, so it means compel.

clue.text: Produced work lacking fluency

definitions.meaning: toiled or did hard work, as in the verb to labour

explanation.surface: A piece of writing that came out clumsily.
explanation.definitionFit: Laboured is the past tense of working hard and also means stilted, done with effort.

clue.text: Try to improve what suspenders do

definitions.meaning: make an effort to do better
garters or sock suspenders hold up hosiery

explanation.surface: Making an effort, the way garters work.
explanation.walkthrough: SUSPENDERS here are the British garters that hold up socks or stockings, not American trouser braces.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means make an effort to do better; suspenders literally keep hosiery from slipping.

clue.text: Ridiculous! Although altered after I went, it's still ridiculous

indicators.note: altered says the remaining letters are rearranged into a new word
after I went says one letter I has departed from the first word

explanation.surface: An exclamation that something absurd stays absurd even after being changed.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove one I from RIDICULOUS ('after I went'), leaving RDICULOUS, then 'altered' rearranges those letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are straightforward synonyms meaning absurd or laughable.

clue.text: Spoils jigsaw, perhaps, that's overturned

indicators.note: overturned in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a jigsaw is a power saw, an example of a tool

explanation.surface: Someone ruins a jigsaw puzzle by knocking it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoils' looks like a verb, but it is the noun meaning plunder; the jigsaw is the saw, not the puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Loot means goods taken in war or by theft, which are spoils.

clue.text: Dissatisfaction with marker attached to canvas

parts.note: a disc can serve as a marker or counter
on means attached to, as a label is on a parcel
a tent is made of canvas, and canvas can mean tents

explanation.surface: Unhappiness with a pen fixed to an artist's canvas.
explanation.definitionFit: Discontent is a direct synonym for dissatisfaction or unhappiness.

clue.text: Game in which press see changes

definitions.text: Game in which press see changes

parts.words: Game in which press see changes
parts.note: a party game where a message is passed along a line in murmurs and gets garbled; the press here are a crowd, not journalists

explanation.surface: Journalists notice how stories alter.
explanation.definitionFit: In this party game a muttered message mutates as people pass it on.

clue.text: Material used in shirt and shoe

definitions.meaning: a woven cotton cloth used for shirts

explanation.surface: Fabric for shirts and footwear.
explanation.definitionFit: The city name labels both a shirting cloth and a classic lace-up shoe.

clue.text: Ice located around the globe

indicators.note: around says one piece is placed round the other

parts.note: set means placed or located
an orb is a globe

explanation.surface: Polar ice found all over the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ice' suggests frozen water or polar caps, but it is the dessert sense, a water ice; 'around' signals the container.
explanation.definitionFit: A sorbet is a water ice, a frozen fruit dessert.

clue.text: Abusive nit endlessly circling one such as Big Ben

indicators.note: circling means the shortened insect wraps round the other pieces
endlessly means the last letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: a nit is the egg or young of a louse, loosely a louse
one is the Roman numeral I
Big Ben is the great bell in the Westminster clock tower

explanation.surface: Calling someone a nit seems rude, set beside the famous London clock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' drops the final E, leaving LOUS, and 'circling' wraps it round the other pieces. Big Ben is strictly the bell, not the tower.
explanation.definitionFit: Libellous statements are defamatory and so abusive of the person they target.

clue.text: Deduce the number escaping fire

indicators.note: escaping means these letters get out of the larger word

parts.note: an inferno is a raging fire
NO is the standard abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A detective works something out about the count of people fleeing a blaze.
explanation.definitionFit: To infer is to conclude from evidence, a direct synonym of deduce.

clue.text: Composer, a French one, in pleasant surroundings

indicators.note: in says the French word sits inside the word for pleasant

parts.note: good means pleasant, and here it forms the surroundings
un is French for a or one

explanation.surface: A musician, a Frenchman, is pictured in agreeable surroundings.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Gounod was the French composer of the opera Faust.

clue.text: Firm measure includes university, it's been realised

definitions.note: past-participle phrase; the answer is the matching verb phrase, 'come true', as in 'it's come true'

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

indicators.note: includes says the measure holds the university letter inside it

parts.note: a metre is a measure of length

explanation.surface: A company's yardstick takes in a university, and something has come to pass.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'it's come true' in place of 'it's been realised': the 'it's' is a link that makes the swap work.
explanation.definitionFit: A hope that comes true is fulfilled, which is to say it is realised.

clue.text: Fit convicts may feel happier here

definitions.meaning: nick is British slang for prison, so a decent one would cheer inmates

explanation.surface: Prisoners prefer a pleasant jail.
explanation.walkthrough: NICK is British slang for a prison or police station.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in good condition, and literally describes a pleasant prison.

clue.text: Had the tenner changed straight away

indicators.note: changed says the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone had a ten-pound note broken into smaller money immediately.
explanation.walkthrough: A TENNER is British slang for a ten-pound note; 'changed' plays on giving change for it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means at that very moment, immediately, without delay.

clue.text: Complete list very quickly

parts.note: full means complete or entire
a ship that lists leans over, that is, it tilts

explanation.surface: Finish the catalogue at great speed.
explanation.definitionFit: At full tilt means at top speed, so the phrase means very quickly.

clue.text: Breaks in new military gear

indicators.note: new suggests the letters of the first word are made anew in a different order

explanation.surface: Someone wears in a fresh piece of army kit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaks in' reads as wearing in new boots, but 'new' rearranges BREAKS to BEARSK, with IN kept as written at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A bearskin is the tall fur cap worn by British Guards regiments as ceremonial dress.

clue.text: Royal retreat hard to find in island -—- mapmakers' practice is to circle

indicators.note: is to circle says the mapmakers and their practice go round the middle part

parts.note: OS is the Ordnance Survey, Britain's national mapping agency
use means custom or practice

indicators.note: to find in says the letter for hard is located inside the island

parts.note: Borneo is a large island in south-east Asia
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A royal hideaway is hard to locate on an island, so surveyors draw a ring round it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To find in' and 'is to circle' are the two container signals, the second wrapping the first. The answer, on the Isle of Wight, was Queen Victoria's seaside home.
explanation.definitionFit: Queen Victoria used this Isle of Wight house as a private royal getaway.

clue.text: Book of the Month — version of the Bible that's old

parts.note: Oct is the abbreviation for October
AV is the Authorised Version, the King James Bible

explanation.surface: A book of the month club offers an old translation of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: Octavo is a book size from sheets folded into eight leaves, hence a book.

clue.text: Little person a maiden, I would communicate with

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
I'd is the contraction of I would
to get someone, as on the phone, is to reach and talk to them

explanation.surface: A small figure and a young woman I'd like to talk to.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, now often considered offensive, refers to a very small person.

clue.text: Money on which police have finally to agree

parts.note: a coin is a piece of money
CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of the British police

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of the following word

explanation.surface: Detectives eventually reach agreement over some cash.
explanation.definitionFit: To coincide is to correspond or be in agreement, as views can coincide.

clue.text: Stable lad Jack's left elbow, and right

indicators.note: Jack's left means the letter for Jack has gone away from the word

parts.note: to elbow someone is to jostle them
J is the card abbreviation for jack

explanation.surface: A young groom called Jack has hurt his left elbow but his right is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack's left' reads as 'Jack has left': J leaves JOSTLE, giving OSTLE, then R is added.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostler looked after the horses at an inn, much as a stable lad does.

clue.text: Correspondence turns up in school

indicators.note: turns up in a down clue means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: a note is a short letter, a piece of correspondence

explanation.surface: A letter appears at a school.
explanation.walkthrough: ETON is the famous English boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College is a well-known English public school.

clue.text: Are English soldiers providing protection?

parts.note: an are is a metric unit of area, abbreviated A
GIs are American soldiers

explanation.surface: A question about whether English troops are offering a defence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Are' looks like a verb, but it is the unit of 100 square metres, symbol A.
explanation.definitionFit: Under someone's aegis means under their protection or sponsorship.

clue.text: 13 huntsmen are

definitions.meaning: the cross-reference points to the answer at 13, meaning in fine condition or healthy
foxhunters wear scarlet coats called pinks, so they are dressed in that colour

explanation.surface: Something about thirteen huntsmen.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in excellent health, matching 13's phrase, and hunting coats are called pink.

clue.text: Frank striving to jog from pole to pole

parts.note: out to, as in 'out to win', means striving to

indicators.note: from pole to pole frames the jog between two compass points

parts.note: S is the South Pole
N is the North Pole
to jog someone is to poke or nudge them

explanation.surface: Someone tries to go running all the way from one end of the earth to the other.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From pole to pole' puts the jog between the two compass poles. 'Out to', as in 'out to win', is idiomatic for striving to.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frank means speaking plainly and candidly, which is being outspoken.

clue.text: Act as a substitute for demonstration

definitions.meaning: to deputise or fill in for someone at a meeting
a protest in which people occupy a place and refuse to move

explanation.surface: Standing in for a demonstration.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit in for someone is to replace them, and a sit-in is an occupation protest.
